en.location: 📍 Near Uitgeest · Open water with reed banks · Small
en.description: Het Die is one of the many North Holland waters carrying that word in their name — die, dieze or diep simply means watercourse or channel, and it is among the oldest water names in Dutch. Such waters are not dug canals but natural peat streams: channels that formed in the peat landscape as surplus rainwater found its way to the sea. They are recognisable by their irregular, winding course, in sharp contrast to the later straight canals. Het Die connects the Uitgeest waters with the Alkmaardermeer. Along the banks stand reed and bulrush, holding reed warbler, reed bunting and marsh harrier; on the water swim great crested grebe and coot.

en.description: The Limmerveentje is a postage stamp of an area — barely a couple of hectares — but it preserves something almost vanished from the whole of Kennemerland: a patch of peat in the beach plain. Between the beach ridges of Limmen and Heiloo peat grew after the sea level rose, and nearly everywhere it was dug away or drained to polder level. Here a hollow remained where the groundwater still stands high and seepage flows in from the beach ridge. That combination of wet, nutrient-poor and lime-rich makes a blue-grassland type vegetation possible, with glaucous sedge, marsh violet and heath spotted orchid. On such a small surface that is a botanical treasure house. Notable dragonflies fly here and reed bunting and whitethroat breed.

nl.description: Een eendenkooi is een van de vernuftigste vangsystemen die de mens ooit bedacht: een vijver met vier gebogen, overkapte vangpijpen, omringd door een dicht kooibos dat volstrekte rust waarborgt. De kooiker lokte wilde eenden met tamme staleenden en met een klein hondje, de kooikershond, dat zich langs schermen liet zien en weer verdween — eenden volgen zo’n verschijning uit nieuwsgierigheid de pijp in. Rond elke kooi gold bovendien het recht van afpaling: binnen een straal van honderden meters mocht niemand lawaai maken of bouwen. Dat wettelijke stilteregime maakt oude kooien tot ecologische eilanden. Hier broeden nu buizerd, boomvalk, ransuil en houtsnip, en in het kooibos groeit een rijke voorjaarsflora.

tags: Duck decoy · historic trapping system with decoy wood
en.location: 📍 Near Uitgeest · Duck decoy with decoy wood · Small
en.description: A duck decoy is one of the most ingenious trapping systems people ever devised: a pond with four curved, netted pipes, surrounded by a dense decoy wood that guarantees absolute quiet. The decoyman lured wild ducks with tame call ducks and with a small dog, the kooikerhondje, which showed itself along screens and vanished again — ducks follow such an apparition into the pipe out of curiosity. Around every decoy the right of enclosure also applied: within a radius of hundreds of metres nobody might make noise or build. That legal regime of silence makes old decoys ecological islands. Buzzard, hobby, long-eared owl and woodcock now breed here, and a rich spring flora grows in the decoy wood.

nl.description: De Dorregeesterpolder is genoemd naar het verdwenen dorpje Dorregeest, en dat achtervoegsel -geest is in Noord-Holland een landschapsaanduiding van de eerste orde: geest betekent hoge, droge zandgrond, van dezelfde stam als gust — onvruchtbaar. Geestgronden zijn de oude strandwallen, en daar stonden de dorpen; het lage veen ertussen was weiland. Dorregeest verdween, maar zijn naam bleef aan de polder hangen. Het wandelpad loopt dwars door de veenweide, langs sloten en over dammetjes — in dit deel van Noord-Holland een zeldzaamheid, want de meeste polders zijn alleen vanaf de weg te zien. Onderweg zie je grutto, tureluur, kievit en slobeend, en in de sloten bloeit in mei de waterviolier.

en.location: 📍 Between Uitgeest and Akersloot · Peat-meadow polder · Medium-sized
en.description: The Dorregeesterpolder is named after the vanished hamlet of Dorregeest, and the suffix -geest is a first-order landscape term in North Holland: geest means high, dry sandy ground, from the same stem as gust — barren. Geest grounds are the old beach ridges, and that is where the villages stood; the low peat in between was pasture. Dorregeest vanished, but its name stuck to the polder. The footpath runs straight through the peat meadow, along ditches and over little dams — a rarity in this part of North Holland, since most polders can only be seen from the road. Along the way you see godwit, redshank, lapwing and shoveler, and in May the water violet flowers in the ditches.

nl.location: 📍 Tussen Alkmaar, Uitgeest en Krommenie · Veenmeer · Groot
nl.description: Het Alkmaardermeer is een van de weinige overgebleven veenmeren van Noord-Holland, en het bestaat nog doordat het niet werd drooggemalen zoals de Beemster, Purmer en Schermer. Zulke meren ontstonden niet natuurlijk maar door turfwinning en golfslag: als er eenmaal open water was, sloegen de golven bij storm steeds meer veenoever weg — een zichzelf versterkend proces dat hele dorpen verzwolg. Toen de wateroverlast onhoudbaar werd, verdween in de zeventiende eeuw het ene na het andere meer onder de molens. Het Alkmaardermeer bleef als boezemwater gespaard. Nu is het een groot open water met rietoevers, moeraslanden en legakkers, waar fuut, aalscholver, zwarte stern en bruine kiekendief broeden en in de winter duizenden watervogels pleisteren.

tags: Lake · peat lake with reed banks and marshland
en.location: 📍 Between Alkmaar, Uitgeest and Krommenie · Peat lake · Large
en.description: The Alkmaardermeer is one of the few surviving peat lakes of North Holland, and it still exists because it was not pumped dry like the Beemster, Purmer and Schermer. Such lakes did not arise naturally but through peat cutting and wave action: once there was open water, storms tore away ever more peat bank — a self-reinforcing process that swallowed whole villages. When the flooding became untenable, one lake after another disappeared beneath the windmills in the seventeenth century. The Alkmaardermeer was spared as storage water. It is now a large open water with reed banks, marshland and peat baulks, where great crested grebe, cormorant, black tern and marsh harrier breed and thousands of waterfowl stage in winter.
en.meta: Best season & peak months: Nov–Feb (waterfowl concentrations), May–Jul (black tern and reed birds) Best time of day: Early morning — mirror-calm water and active birds.

Het aangrenzende Huldtoneel heeft een veel oudere naam met een verrassende betekenis: een huldtoneel of huldigingstoneel was de plek waar de heer van het gebied door zijn onderdanen werd gehuldigd — een openbare ceremoniële weide waar trouw werd gezworen. Zulke plekken lagen buiten het kasteel, in het open veld, zodat iedereen kon toekijken. Ecologisch is het landgoed nu vooral waardevol om zijn oude parkbomen op de strandwal en de natte weilanden erachter. Er broeden boomklever, grote bonte specht, bosuil en gekraagde roodstaart, en in het voorjaar bloeit een rijke stinzenflora.

tags: Estate · castle woodland and old meadows
en.location: 📍 Heemskerk · Castle estate · Medium-sized
en.description: The Marquette estate at Heemskerk centres on a medieval castle converted into a country seat in the seventeenth century; it took its name from a French owner. The adjoining Huldtoneel has a far older name with a surprising meaning: a huldtoneel or homage ground was the place where the lord of the district was paid homage by his subjects — a public ceremonial meadow where allegiance was sworn. Such places lay outside the castle, in the open field, so that everyone could watch. Ecologically the estate is now valuable above all for its old park trees on the beach ridge and the wet meadows behind. Nuthatch, great spotted woodpecker, tawny owl and redstart breed here, and a rich stinzen flora flowers in spring.

Bus of bosch spreekt voor zich, maar vroon is een juridische term uit de vroege middeleeuwen: het betekent heerlijk bezit, grond die aan de landsheer toebehoorde. Vroonlanden waren vaak woeste gronden — duinen, moerassen, meren — die niemand kon ontginnen en die daarom bij de graaf bleven. De naam Vroonmeer bewaart dus het bezitsrecht van een meer dat allang verland is. Wat resteert is een vochtige laagte in de duinrand, met elzen- en wilgenstruweel en veenmosrijke plekken. tags: Dune edge · copse and silted-up dune lake
en.location: 📍 Between Heemskerk and the dunes · Dune-edge wood with hollow · Small
en.description: Weijenbus and Vroonmeer lie on the transition from the inner dune edge to the beach plain, and both names are old. Bus or bosch speaks for itself, but vroon is a legal term from the early Middle Ages: it means seigneurial property, land belonging to the territorial lord. Vroon lands were often waste grounds — dunes, marshes, lakes — that nobody could reclaim and which therefore stayed with the count. The name Vroonmeer thus preserves the ownership right to a lake long since silted up. What remains is a damp hollow in the dune edge, with alder and willow scrub and sphagnum-rich patches. Nightingale, grasshopper warbler and great spotted woodpecker breed here, and orchids grow in the hollow.

De stelling werkte niet met muren maar met water: bij dreiging zou een ring van polders onder water worden gezet, precies diep genoeg om onbegaanbaar te zijn voor infanterie maar te ondiep voor boten. De forten bewaakten de accessen — de dijken en wegen die boven het inundatiewater uitstaken. Militair is er nooit uit geschoten. tags: Defence Line of Amsterdam · fort with moat and fort wood
en.location: 📍 Krommeniedijk, on the Defence Line of Amsterdam · Fort grounds · Small
en.description: Fort Krommeniedijk forms part of the Defence Line of Amsterdam, the 135-kilometre ring of 42 forts built around the capital between 1880 and 1920 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996. The line worked not with walls but with water: in an emergency a ring of polders would be flooded, exactly deep enough to be impassable for infantry but too shallow for boats. The forts guarded the accesses — the dikes and roads standing above the inundation water. Militarily, not a shot was ever fired from them. What remains is a concrete fort in a moat with fort wood, and the thick walls are now a winter roost for bats. Kingfisher, barn owl and treecreeper breed on the grounds.
en.meta: Best season & peak months: Apr–Jun (breeding birds and fort wood), Oct–Mar (hibernating bats) Best time of day: Dusk — bats then leave the fort.

en.location: 📍 Between Krommenie and Uitgeest · Peat meadow with marsh · Large
en.description: Ham en Crommenije is an extensive peat-meadow area with two eloquent names. Ham is an old landscape word for a bend or corner of land in a watercourse — the same word found in English place names ending in -ham. Crommenije is compounded from krom, crooked, and IJ: the crooked arm of the IJ that once reached inland here. Both names therefore describe water that is no longer there. What remains is one of the largest continuous peat-meadow areas in North Holland, with wet grasslands, turf pits and reed fringes partly managed as marsh nature. It is one of the province’s most important meadow-bird areas, with godwit, redshank, ruff and snipe, while marsh harrier and Savi’s warbler breed in the reed zones.

tags: City park · old coppice wood on the beach ridge
en.location: 📍 Beverwijk · Historic wood and park · Small
en.description: Westerhout in Beverwijk is one of the oldest woods in Kennemerland, and the word hout in the name is telling: in Middle Dutch hout simply meant wood, and it appears in dozens of names from Haarlemmerhout to ’s-Gravenhout. Those old woods on the beach ridges were managed as coppice: every eight to fifteen years the stools were cut back, after which they resprouted — a harvesting system that yielded firewood and utility wood without killing the tree, and which can make stools centuries old. Westerhout was converted into a public park in the nineteenth century, but the ancient soil remained. As a result a rich spring flora of bluebell and ramsons grows there, and nuthatch, tawny owl and great spotted woodpecker breed.

tags: Defence work · earthen lunettes with moat
en.location: 📍 Near Beverwijk · Historic earthworks · Small
en.description: The Lunetten near Beverwijk are small, self-contained defence works with a characteristic shape: a lunette has two forward-facing points and an open rear, giving a plan resembling a half-moon — hence the name, from the French lune. They were built in the nineteenth century as part of the defence of the North Sea Canal area, to cover the approach to the Defence Line of Amsterdam. Unlike the later concrete forts, lunettes consist entirely of earth and grass: ramparts, moats and slopes. That is exactly what makes them ecologically attractive, for the steep, never-fertilised banks carry a poor vegetation rich in flowers. Butterflies and wild bees fly here, and amphibians live in the moats.

en.location: 📍 Near Heemskerk, on the Defence Line of Amsterdam · Fort grounds · Small
en.description: Fort Veldhuis is one of the forts of the Defence Line of Amsterdam and today houses a museum about the air war over North Holland. That suits the place, for the Line’s forts were obsolete even before they were finished: by around 1920 it was clear that aircraft and heavy artillery could simply pass over a water line. The entire ring was thus a defensive system that never worked — and precisely for that reason survived intact. The fort grounds consist of a concrete main building, a moat and dense planting that once served as camouflage. That combination now yields rich urban-fringe nature: bats in the cellars, kingfisher at the moat, and treecreeper, green woodpecker and redstart in the fort wood.

Het waterbeheer was daarbij verrassend fijnzinnig — om het gewenste peil van dertig tot veertig centimeter te bereiken moest het water in compartimenten worden gehouden, elk met eigen sluizen en dammen. tags: Dike system · flower-rich verges of the Defence Line
en.location: 📍 Between the forts of the Defence Line of Amsterdam · Dike ribbons · Medium-sized
en.description: The Liniedijken are the earthen connections between the forts of the Defence Line of Amsterdam, and they played a double role: they held the inundation water at the right level and served as a sheltered supply route for troops and equipment. The water management was surprisingly subtle — to reach the desired depth of thirty to forty centimetres the water had to be kept in compartments, each with its own sluices and dams. That is exactly why the dike system runs so erratically through the landscape. Ecologically the dikes are now long linear landscape elements: poor, never-fertilised verges working as a corridor between the fort woods. Knapweed, wild marjoram and quaking grass flower here, and many butterflies, bees and grasshoppers fly.
en.meta: Best season & peak months: Jun–Aug (verge flowering and insects), Sep–Oct (migrants along the ribbons) Best time of day: Warm afternoon — insects on the sunny dike slopes.

en.description: Fort St. Aagtendijk is named after the dike it stands on, and that Sint-Aagtendijk is centuries older than the fort: it was built in the Middle Ages to protect Kennemerland from the waters of the IJ, and is named after Saint Agatha, whose convent lay nearby. When the Defence Line of Amsterdam was built around 1900, such existing dikes were deliberately chosen: they stood above the future inundation water and were therefore accesses that had to be guarded. So at this spot two water defences six hundred years apart lie one on top of the other. The fort grounds are now a nature area with moat, earthen ramparts and fort wood, with bats in the cellars and kingfisher, green woodpecker and treecreeper on the site.

en.description: The Wijkeroogpark stands on the site of the vanished village of Wijk aan het IJ, which had to make way in the nineteenth century for the digging of the North Sea Canal. That canal, cut between 1865 and 1876, sliced straight through Kennemerland and changed the district more profoundly than any other intervention: the IJ was closed off, the dunes breached at IJmuiden and whole polders raised with the excavated sand. The park was laid out on such raised ground, which explains the soil — lime-rich sea sand, on which a surprisingly rich flora grows. Beneath the now mature trees stinzen flora blooms, and green woodpecker, nuthatch and redstart breed. From the canal bank, seagoing ships pass at arm’s length.

Dat kalkgehalte is beslissend: de Hollandse duinen ten zuiden van Bergen bestaan uit jong, schelprijk zand, waardoor er een totaal andere en veel soortenrijkere vegetatie groeit dan in de kalkarme Waddenduinen. en.location: 📍 Between IJmuiden, Bloemendaal and Zandvoort · Dunes · Very large
en.description: Zuid-Kennemerland National Park covers thirty-six square kilometres of dune between the North Sea Canal and Zandvoort and is one of the best-preserved lime-rich dune areas in north-west Europe. That lime content is decisive: the Holland dunes south of Bergen consist of young, shell-rich sand, producing a wholly different and far more species-rich vegetation than the lime-poor Wadden dunes. In the dune slacks orchids and grass-of-Parnassus flower, on the dry slopes dune pansy and kidney vetch. Since the 1990s Highland cattle, konik horses and European bison have grazed here — the last since 2007 in the Kraansvlak, the first bison project in western Europe. Nightingale, wheatear, woodlark and goshawk breed.

The park is an English landscape garden with winding ponds, little bridges and very old beeches. Ecologically it is about the old trees with cavities: nuthatch, tawny owl and great spotted woodpecker breed, and bats roost there.

en.description: Schoonenberg, Hoogergeest and Lievendaal are three adjoining country seats that together show how Kennemerland’s estate zone works. The names tell the story: Schoonenberg and Hoogergeest refer to the high, dry sandy ground of the beach ridge — geest is exactly that — while Lievendaal names the lower, damp side. Within a few hundred metres, then, the soil shifts from dry dune sand to wet beach plain, and that is what makes the zone so ecologically rich. On the high parts grow beech and oak woods with stinzen flora, on the low parts alder carr with marsh marigold. Nuthatch, tawny owl and green woodpecker breed, and many bats live here.

tags: Country seat · garden-history monument with three styles
en.location: 📍 Velsen-Zuid · Historic country seat · Medium-sized
en.description: Beeckestijn is Kennemerland’s most famous country seat and, in garden-history terms, the most important in the Netherlands, for the garden preserves three style periods side by side. Close to the house the crisp formal baroque layout from the early eighteenth century survives, with straight avenues and symmetrical parterres. Behind it follows the early landscape style laid out by the architect Johann Georg Michael around 1770 — one of the first in the Netherlands, with winding paths and sight lines. And at the far end lies a nineteenth-century extension. That layering made it a national monument in 1972. Ecologically the very old beeches and oaks count most: nuthatch, tawny owl, green woodpecker and redstart breed, and bats roost in the cavities.

tags: Defence Line of Amsterdam · fort in a drained lake polder
en.location: 📍 Near Velsen-Zuid · Fort grounds with moat · Small
en.description: Fort Zuidwijkermeer stands in the Zuidwijkermeerpolder, and that name preserves the lake that lay here before the draining. This makes the location paradoxical: the fort was to defend a polder by flooding it again — with precisely the water that generations earlier had been pumped out with such effort. That is how the whole Defence Line of Amsterdam worked: the inundation fields were Holland’s most fertile farmland, and in wartime they would be deliberately sacrificed. The fort itself is a concrete structure from around 1900, surrounded by a moat and dense planting. That combination now yields valuable nature: bats hibernate in the cellars, the kingfisher breeds in the moat bank, and flower-rich vegetation grows on the site.

tags: City wood · young woodland on marine clay
en.location: 📍 Heerhugowaard · City wood · Medium-sized
en.description: The Waarderhout is a young wood on the edge of Heerhugowaard, planted to give the fast-growing town a green lung. The name combines waard — land surrounded by water, the same word as in Heerhugowaard itself — with hout, the old word for wood. The soil is remarkable: this is a drained lake polder, pumped dry in 1631, and the ground consists of heavy marine clay lying four metres below sea level. Planting woodland on such wet clay is difficult — roots suffocate quickly — so the wood was laid out with ditches, raised beds and species that tolerate wet feet: ash, alder, willow and poplar. It is now mature enough for great spotted woodpecker, treecreeper, long-eared owl and goshawk, and many fungi grow here.

en.description: The Westbeverkoog carries two meaningful words. Koog is a North Holland and Frisian landscape term for land outside the dike — ground lying seaward of the dike that flooded at high water and was later empoldered; the same word found in Koog aan de Zaan. And bever, beaver, recalls that this animal was once common in the Holland peat marshes, until hunting eliminated it in the sixteenth century — it only returned to the Netherlands in 1988. The area is now an open peat-meadow polder with broad ditches and reed fringes. It matters for meadow birds, with godwit, redshank and lapwing, and in winter for geese and wigeon. Water soldier grows in the ditches, on which the green hawker lays its eggs.

en.location: 📍 Between Avenhorn, Schermerhorn and Ursem · Peat meadow · Large
en.description: The Mijzenpolder is a rarity: a large peat-meadow area that was never dug away or pumped dry. All around lie the famous drained lake polders — Beemster, Schermer, Heerhugowaard — but the Mijzen stayed as it was, on the original peat layer. As a result the ground level here is higher than in the surrounding polders, and the old strip parcelling from the medieval reclamation is still fully legible: long narrow parcels at right angles to a reclamation axis. Because the water level stayed high and fertilisation low, this is one of the best meadow-bird areas in North Holland, with high densities of godwit, redshank, lapwing and shoveler. Water violet flowers in the ditches and water soldier grows there.

en.location: 📍 Between Hoorn and Scharwoude, on the Markermeer · Foreland grassland · Small
en.description: De Hulk lies outside the dike on the Markermeer, and the name is an old sea word: a hulk was a heavy, broad cargo ship, but in landscape names it indicates a bend or curve in the coastline. Here the old West Frisian Ring Dike does indeed make a sharp turn. The foreland arose through silting against the dike, and such strips are ecologically notable because they were never fertilised or ploughed up. Since the closing of the Zuiderzee the water has turned fresh, but the salt flora has partly persisted on the highest parts. It is an important place for waders: avocet, redshank and oystercatcher breed there, and godwits and ruffs rest during migration.

en.location: 📍 Along the Markermeer near Hoorn · Foreland strips · Small
en.description: The Uiterdijken are the narrow strips of land between the sea dike and the water, and the word is related to uiterwaard, floodplain: uiter means outermost, the land lying outside the dike. In Zuiderzee days these strips were salt or brackish salt marshes that regularly flooded in storms; farmers used them as summer pasture and accepted that winter would submerge them. After the Afsluitdijk (1932) the water turned fresh and within decades the vegetation changed from saline to reed. What remains is a linear ribbon of nature along the entire coast, making it exceptionally valuable as a migration corridor. Sedge warbler, reed warbler, bluethroat and bearded reedling breed, and geese and swans forage in winter.

en.location: 📍 Along the West Frisian Ring Dike · Foreland grassland · Small
en.description: The Kogen are forelands along the old Zuiderzee coast, and the name is the plural of koog: land lying outside the dike that floods at high water. The word occurs frequently in North Holland and on the Wadden islands. Koog lands formed as silt settled against the sea dike; as the strip grew higher, salt-marsh vegetation established and it could serve as summer pasture. Often such a koog was in time embanked, after which a new koog formed outside the new dike — a cycle that built up the North Holland coastline step by step. The present Kogen are freshwater grasslands with ditches and reed edges, where redshank, avocet and oystercatcher breed and geese forage in winter.

en.location: 📍 Between Graft-De Rijp, Driehuizen and Schermerhorn · Peat meadow · Large
en.description: The Eilandspolder owes its name to its position: it is literally an island of undug peat, surrounded by the deep drained polders of the Schermer and Beemster. When those lakes were pumped dry in the seventeenth century, this strip was left — and precisely for that reason it is one of the finest examples of medieval peat reclamation landscape in the Netherlands. The pattern of long, narrow parcels separated by ditches has scarcely changed since the twelfth century, and many parcels are reachable only by boat. That inaccessibility is its ecological strength: it is a Natura 2000 site and a prime area for meadow and marsh birds, with godwit, redshank, snipe, purple heron and root vole.

en.location: 📍 Western side of the Eilandspolder near Grootschermer · Peat meadow · Medium-sized
en.description: The Westelijke Eilandspolder is the wettest part of the peat island, and it is here that management is most nature-oriented. Where the eastern side is still largely agricultural meadow-bird land, here lies a mosaic of reedland, rough vegetation, turf pits and floating mats — rafts of vegetation growing on the water that you can barely walk on. Such succession stages have become rare in the Netherlands, for they arise only when the water level moves with the seasons instead of being kept artificially flat. It provides habitat for species disappearing elsewhere: bittern, Savi’s warbler, bearded reedling and purple heron, while rare sedges and orchids grow in the sphagnum reedlands.

Het gebied werd in de elfde en twaalfde eeuw ontgonnen en behield sindsdien zijn structuur. Wat het bijzonder maakt is de openheid: er staan nauwelijks bomen of gebouwen, waardoor weidevogels vrij zicht hebben op naderende predatoren — een voorwaarde die veel Nederlandse polders inmiddels verloren hebben. en.description: De Zeevang is a vast, ruler-flat peat-meadow polder between Edam and the Markermeer, and the name is remarkably old: vang means enclosed or embanked area — the same word as in vangen, to catch — so Zeevang literally means ‘land won from the sea and diked in’. The area was reclaimed in the eleventh and twelfth centuries and has kept its structure ever since. What makes it special is its openness: there are hardly any trees or buildings, so meadow birds have a clear view of approaching predators — a condition many Dutch polders have now lost. It is a Natura 2000 site, important for godwit, redshank and lapwing and in winter for thousands of wigeon and white-fronted geese.

nl.description: De Westwouderpolder draagt in zijn naam de herinnering aan iets wat volledig verdwenen is: woud. Voordat de veenontginningen begonnen was het Hollandse veenmoeras deels bedekt met een moerasbos van els, berk en wilg, en de ontginners noemden hun nieuwe nederzettingen naar wat ze er aantroffen — Westwoud, Oostwoud, Zwaagdijk. In deze polder is het beheer nu op weidevogels gericht, met plas-drasgebieden: percelen die in het voorjaar bewust onder een laagje water worden gezet, zodat steltlopers er met hun snavel bij de bodemdieren kunnen. Dat trekt grutto, tureluur, kemphaan en watersnip, en in de trektijd allerlei doortrekkers.

en.location: 📍 Near Beets and Oosthuizen · Peat meadow · Medium-sized
en.description: The Westwouderpolder carries in its name the memory of something entirely vanished: woud, forest. Before the peat reclamations began, the Holland peat marsh was partly covered by a swamp forest of alder, birch and willow, and the reclaimers named their new settlements after what they found — Westwoud, Oostwoud, Zwaagdijk. When the peat was drained the forest disappeared within a few generations, leaving open pasture. In this polder management is now aimed at meadow birds, with plas-dras areas: parcels deliberately flooded in spring under a shallow film of water so waders can reach soil invertebrates with their bills. That draws godwit, redshank, ruff and snipe, and all sorts of migrants in passage.

en.location: 📍 Markenbinnen, on the Defence Line of Amsterdam · Fort grounds · Small
en.description: Fort Marken Binnen lies by the hamlet of Markenbinnen, and that name has nothing to do with the island of Marken: marke is an old word for border district or common land, cognate with German Mark and English march in the sense of a borderland. The fort was built around 1900 to guard the dike along the Alkmaardermeer — one of the few high lines through the future inundation zone. Because the site was then barely used for a century, a dense fort wood developed around it with a moat encircling it. That is now its natural value: bats hibernate in the cool, humidity-stable cellars, and kingfisher, treecreeper, green woodpecker and tawny owl breed on the grounds.

Ecologisch is het een verlengstuk van het moerasgebied Ham en Crommenije: er broeden rietzanger, snor, bruine kiekendief en watersnip, en in de sloten groeit krabbenscheer met de groene glazenmaker.

en.location: 📍 Between Krommenie and the Alkmaardermeer · Peat meadow · Medium-sized
en.description: The Krommenieërwoudpolder is a name stacking three landscape layers on top of one another: Krommenie for the crooked arm of the IJ, woud for the vanished peat swamp forest, and polder for the pumping that made the whole habitable. To read the name is to read three hundred years of landscape history. The area lies low and wet at the edge of the Alkmaardermeer and has never been intensively used. It therefore consists of a mosaic of wet grasslands, reed fringes and ditches with a high water level. Ecologically it is an extension of the Ham en Crommenije marsh: sedge warbler, Savi’s warbler, marsh harrier and snipe breed, and water soldier grows in the ditches with the green hawker.

en.location: 📍 Spijkerboor, on the Beemster ring canal · Fort grounds · Small
en.description: Fort bij Spijkerboor is the largest and most heavily armed fort of the Defence Line of Amsterdam, and there is a reason: three important accesses crossed here — the Beemster ring canal, the Westdijk and the road to Purmerend. Where several high lines met the defence had to be strongest, and so this fort alone received two armoured gun turrets with guns that could fire far into the inundation zone. In the Second World War the fort was still used as a prison. It is now a monument with extensive grounds, and the thick concrete corridors form one of the most important bat hibernacula in North Holland. Kingfisher, green woodpecker and barn owl breed on the site.

en.description: The Fort aan de Jisperweg stands in the middle of the Beemster, the polder drained in 1612 and listed as UNESCO World Heritage for its perfectly rational layout: a grid of straight roads and canals based on Renaissance ideals about the ideal ordering of space. That the fort stands within it is doubly remarkable, for here two World Heritage sites touch — the Beemster and the Defence Line of Amsterdam. The contrast is sharp: the Beemster is a monument to draining, the fort an instrument for flooding it all again. The fort grounds are now a green island in the crisp grid landscape, with moat, ramparts and dense planting. Bats hibernate here and kingfisher, treecreeper and green woodpecker breed.

Rond veel forten leverde dat karakteristieke houten Kringenwetboerderijen op, en het verklaart waarom de omgeving nog altijd opvallend open en onbebouwd is. Die openheid is nu een ecologische kwaliteit: het fortbos ligt als geïsoleerd bosje in een leeg polderlandschap en trekt daardoor veel trekvogels aan. In de kelders overwinteren vleermuizen.

tags: Defence Line of Amsterdam · fort with open field of fire
en.location: 📍 On the Middenweg in the Beemster · Fort grounds · Small
en.description: The Fort aan de Middenweg guarded the central axis of the Beemster, and it illustrates a principle that applied to all the forts but is especially visible here: the Kringenwet, the Zones Act. That law of 1853 forbade building in stone within a radius of three hundred to a thousand metres around a fort — only timber was allowed, so that everything could be swiftly burnt down in an attack to clear the field of fire. Around many forts this produced characteristic timber Zones Act farmhouses, and it explains why the surroundings are still strikingly open and unbuilt. That openness is now an ecological quality: the fort wood lies as an isolated copse in an empty polder landscape and therefore attracts many migrant birds. Bats hibernate in the cellars.

nl.description: Het Kwadijkker Vlot ontleent zijn naam aan twee elementen. Kwadijk is het dorp, en dat betekent letterlijk ‘kwade dijk’ — een dijkvak dat berucht was om zijn doorbraken, want kwaad had in het Middelnederlands de betekenis van slecht of onbetrouwbaar. En vlot is een landschapsterm voor drijvend land: veenpakketten die zo licht en waterverzadigd zijn dat ze bij hoog water meestijgen. Wie erover loopt voelt de bodem deinen. Zulke trilvenen zijn zeldzaam geworden, want ze verdwijnen zodra het peil wordt vastgezet. Hier is het bewaard gebleven als nat grasland met veenmosrijke randen. Er broeden watersnip, tureluur en rietgors, en er groeien zeggen, veenpluis en orchideeën.
nl.meta: Beste seizoen & piekmaanden: Apr–jun (weidevogels), mei–jul (veenflora en orchideeën) Beste tijd van de dag: Vroege ochtend — baltsende watersnippen boven het vlot.

Vlot = drijvend land dat bij hoog water meestijgt.
Zulke trilvenen verdwijnen zodra het peil wordt vastgezet.

Apr–Jun 🐦 Tureluur en rietgors broeden.
Mei–Jun 🌿 Veenpluis pluist wit uit.
Jun–Jul 🌼 Orchideeën in de veenmosranden.
trailheads: Parkeren bij Kwadijk; kijk vanaf de paden aan de rand.
Betreed het vlot niet — het draagt nauwelijks en is kwetsbaar.
Juni voor de orchideeën aan de randen.

tags: Peat meadow · wet grassland with floating banks
en.location: 📍 Near Kwadijk, north of Purmerend · Peat meadow · Small
en.description: The Kwadijkker Vlot takes its name from two elements. Kwadijk is the village, and it means literally ‘bad dike’ — a stretch notorious for its breaches, since kwaad in Middle Dutch meant bad or unreliable. And vlot is a landscape term for floating land: peat layers so light and waterlogged that they rise with high water. Walking on it, you feel the ground sway. Such quaking fens have become rare, for they vanish as soon as the water level is fixed. Here it survives as wet grassland with sphagnum-rich edges. Snipe, redshank and reed bunting breed, and sedges, cottongrass and orchids grow.
en.meta: Best season & peak months: Apr–Jun (meadow birds), May–Jul (bog flora and orchids) Best time of day: Early morning — drumming snipe above the floating land.
why_visit: Kwadijk = ‘bad dike’, notorious for its breaches.
Vlot = floating land that rises with high water.
Such quaking fens vanish as soon as the level is fixed.
Preserved as wet grassland with sphagnum-rich edges.
periodic_phenomena: Mar–Apr 🐦 Snipe drums above the floating land.
Apr–Jun 🐦 Redshank and reed bunting breed.
May–Jun 🌿 Cottongrass turns white.
Jun–Jul 🌼 Orchids in the sphagnum edges.
trailheads: Park at Kwadijk; watch from the paths along the edge.
Do not walk onto the vlot — it barely bears weight and is fragile.
June for the orchids along the edges.
en.footer: 🐶 Dogs not allowed · 💶 Free · ⚠️ Very fragile quaking fen · 🥾 Very wet

tags: Stelling van Amsterdam · noordelijkste fort van de linie
nl.location: 📍 Bij Edam, aan het Markermeer · Fortterrein · Klein
nl.description: Fort Edam is het noordelijkste fort van de Stelling van Amsterdam en sluit de ring af tegen de voormalige Zuiderzee. Die positie was strategisch cruciaal: hier eindigde de inundatielinie tegen open water, en een vijand die de zeedijk zou volgen kon alleen langs dit punt. Het fort bewaakte dus letterlijk het eindpunt van de linie. Interessant is dat de bouwers hier een probleem hadden dat elders niet speelde: de zeedijk zelf mocht niet worden verzwakt, dus het fort staat er vlak naast in plaats van erop. Het terrein bestaat uit een betonnen gebouw met gracht en beplanting, gelegen tussen dijk en polder. Er overwinteren vleermuizen, en op het terrein broeden groene specht, boomkruiper en gekraagde roodstaart.
nl.meta: Beste seizoen & piekmaanden: Apr–jun (broedvogels), okt–mrt (vleermuizen en watervogels op het Markermeer) Beste tijd van de dag: Schemer — vleermuizen en zicht over het Markermeer.

tags: Defence Line of Amsterdam · northernmost fort of the line
en.location: 📍 Near Edam, on the Markermeer · Fort grounds · Small
en.description: Fort Edam is the northernmost fort of the Defence Line of Amsterdam and closes the ring against the former Zuiderzee. That position was strategically crucial: here the inundation line ended against open water, and an enemy following the sea dike could only pass at this point. The fort therefore literally guarded the end point of the line. Interestingly, the builders faced a problem that did not arise elsewhere: the sea dike itself must not be weakened, so the fort stands beside it rather than on it. The site consists of a concrete building with moat and planting, set between dike and polder. Bats hibernate here, and green woodpecker, treecreeper and redstart breed on the grounds.
en.meta: Best season & peak months: Apr–Jun (breeding birds), Oct–Mar (bats and waterfowl on the Markermeer) Best time of day: Dusk — bats and views over the Markermeer.
why_visit: The northernmost fort — closing the ring against the Zuiderzee.
Guarded the end point of the inundation line at open water.
Stands beside the sea dike, which must not be weakened.
Now a bat roost with views over the Markermeer.
periodic_phenomena: Oct–Mar 🦇 Bats hibernate in the fort.
Apr–Jun 🐦 Redstart in the old trees.
Nov–Feb 🦆 Waterfowl on the adjoining Markermeer.
Sep–Oct 🐦 Migration along the dike and fort wood.
wildlife: 🦆 Tufted duck · Wigeon · Great crested grebe on the Markermeer
trailheads: Park at Edam; grounds and dike can be walked.
Climb the sea dike for views over the Markermeer.
Combine with the Uiterdijken along the same dike.

tags: Veenweide · Natura 2000 · grootste aaneengesloten veenweide van West-Europa
nl.location: 📍 Tussen Wormer, Jisp en Wormerveer · Veenweide · Zeer groot
nl.description: Het Wormer- en Jisperveld is met ruim tweeduizend hectare het grootste aaneengesloten veenweidegebied van West-Europa, en het is een landschap dat je vooral vanaf het water begrijpt. Het bestaat uit honderden smalle percelen gescheiden door sloten, en het overgrote deel is alleen per boot bereikbaar — de boeren varen hun koeien nog steeds naar de wei. Dat verklaart waarom het gebied zo gaaf is gebleven: schaalvergroting is er letterlijk onmogelijk zonder het slotenpatroon te dempen. Het waterpeil is hoog en de bemesting laag, en dat maakt het tot een van de belangrijkste weidevogelgebieden van Nederland, met duizenden broedparen grutto, tureluur, kievit en slobeend, plus moerasvogels als roerdomp en purperreiger.
nl.meta: Beste seizoen & piekmaanden: Apr–jun (weidevogeltop), nov–feb (ganzen en smienten) Beste tijd van de dag: Vroege ochtend — het weidevogelkoor is hier op zijn overweldigendst.

tags: Peat meadow · Natura 2000 · largest continuous peat meadow in western Europe
en.location: 📍 Between Wormer, Jisp and Wormerveer · Peat meadow · Very large
en.description: At more than two thousand hectares, the Wormer- en Jisperveld is the largest continuous peat-meadow area in western Europe, and it is a landscape you understand best from the water. It consists of hundreds of narrow parcels separated by ditches, and the great majority is reachable only by boat — farmers still ferry their cows out to pasture. That explains why the area has stayed so intact: scaling up is literally impossible without filling in the ditch pattern. The water level is high and fertilisation low, making it one of the most important meadow-bird areas in the Netherlands, with thousands of breeding pairs of godwit, redshank, lapwing and shoveler, plus marsh birds such as bittern and purple heron.
en.meta: Best season & peak months: Apr–Jun (meadow-bird peak), Nov–Feb (geese and wigeon) Best time of day: Early morning — the meadow-bird chorus is at its most overwhelming here.
why_visit: At 2000 hectares the largest continuous peat meadow in western Europe.

tags: Stadsbos · jong bos in een droogmakerij
nl.location: 📍 Tussen Purmerend en Ilpendam · Stadsbos · Groot
nl.description: Het Purmerbos is in de jaren zeventig aangelegd in de Purmer, het meer dat in 1622 werd drooggemalen. Het hoort tot een generatie bossen die na de oorlog met een expliciet sociaal doel werden geplant: de Randstadgroenstructuur moest de snel groeiende steden recreatieruimte geven, en er werd bewust gekozen voor snel groeiende soorten zoals populier en es om binnen één mensenleven resultaat te hebben. Dat werkte: het bos is nu volwassen en verrassend gevarieerd, met open plekken, waterpartijen en oude lanen. Op de zware kleibodem groeit een rijke ondergroei, en het bos herbergt inmiddels havik, ransuil, grote bonte specht en boomklever. In de herfst is het rijk aan paddenstoelen, en er leven reeën en vossen.

tags: City wood · young woodland in a drained lake polder
en.location: 📍 Between Purmerend and Ilpendam · City wood · Large
en.description: The Purmerbos was planted in the 1970s in the Purmer, the lake pumped dry in 1622. It belongs to a generation of woodlands planted after the war with an explicit social purpose: the Randstad green structure was to give the fast-growing cities recreational space, and fast-growing species such as poplar and ash were deliberately chosen to achieve results within a single lifetime. It worked: the wood is now mature and surprisingly varied, with clearings, water features and old avenues. A rich understorey grows on the heavy clay soil, and the wood now holds goshawk, long-eared owl, great spotted woodpecker and nuthatch. In autumn it is rich in fungi, and roe deer and foxes live here.
en.meta: Best season & peak months: Apr–Jun (song and spring green), Sep–Nov (fungi) Best time of day: Early morning — quiet before the town comes out.
